en: The national flower, sampaguita, blooms with fragrant white petals that open at night and close during the day.
The Philippine eagle, our national bird, has a distinctive crest of long, dark brown feathers on its head that it can raise or flatten.
The Ifugao people carved the Banaue Rice Terraces into the mountains by following the natural contours of the land to trap rainwater for farming.
During the Pahiyas Festival in Lucban, locals decorate their houses with colorful kiping, which are leaf-shaped wafers made from ground rice and natural food coloring.
The Narra tree, the national tree of the Philippines, drops its small, winged seed pods to the ground after its bright yellow flowers bloom.
Marine biologist Angel Alcala observed that establishing protected marine areas allows coral reefs in places like Apo Island to visibly regenerate and thrive.
Volcanic ash from Mount Pinatubo's 1991 eruption mixed with heavy monsoon rains to form massive, observable lahar flows that reshaped Central Luzon's rivers.
T'boli weavers of Lake Sebu extract natural dyes from local plants and roots to color the abaca fibers used for their traditional t'nalak cloth.
The carabao, our national animal, cools its body during hot days by wallowing in mud, which also protects its skin from harsh sunlight and insects.
A common civic duty in Filipino barangays is participating in waste segregation, where households separate biodegradable kitchen scraps from non-biodegradable plastics for collection.
The historic Balete tree in Malolos is a massive banyan tree with hanging aerial roots where locals gathered to hear speeches during the revolutionary period.
The Panagbenga Festival in Baguio City celebrates local flowers, featuring observable parade floats decorated with thousands of real pine needles and fresh blossoms.
